opus-5.5.text:
I think data is one of the central inputs, alongside compute and algorithms, and the way it matters is changing. For most of the past decade the story was fairly simple: take more internet text, train bigger models on it, and capabilities improve in a fairly predictable way. The scaling laws told us how much data you want for a given amount of compute, and for a while there was plenty of high-quality text available.

That's becoming less true. When we've looked at the stock of publicly available human-generated text, it's large but finite. At current rates of scaling, frontier labs are getting close to using a meaningful fraction of it. So the question becomes: what happens when you can't just keep scraping more of the web?

For complex reasoning specifically, I think the answer is that the most valuable data increasingly isn't passive text at all. Internet text is a pretty noisy signal for reasoning. You see the final answer of a proof or a piece of code, but rarely the messy search process behind it: false starts, checking, backtracking. What seems to work much better is data you generate yourself, in domains where you can verify correctness. Math, programming, formal problems, anything with a checker. The model attempts a problem, you check whether it got it right, and you reinforce the successful reasoning. That turns compute into data. It's a bit like the AlphaGo story, where self-play let the system go beyond the human games it started from.

So I'd frame it this way: data is still crucial, but the bottleneck is shifting from "how much human text exists" to "how cheaply can we generate high-quality, verifiable training signal." In domains with good verifiers, I expect rapid progress, because you can essentially buy more data with more compute. The harder open question is the fuzzier domains, like long-horizon real-world tasks, research taste, judgment calls, where it's expensive or slow to know whether an answer was good. How well reasoning learned in verifiable domains transfers to those messier ones is, I think, one of the most important empirical questions for where capabilities go next.

r001.rationale: The response calls data a central input and says it remains crucial, but does not say it may be the most important factor for any specific tasks.

r002.rationale: It identifies generated, high-quality, verifiable training data as especially valuable for complex reasoning and says checking and reinforcing successful attempts can improve it.

r003.rationale: It describes models attempting problems, checking correctness, and reinforcing successful reasoning, which communicates training from reasoning attempts toward correct answers.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think data has been genuinely central, but the way it matters has shifted over time, and it's worth separating out a few different things.

For most of the deep learning era, the story was fairly simple: you scale compute, you scale parameters, and you scale the amount of data you train on, and the scaling laws tell you roughly how much performance you get. Data in that regime is mostly about volume. You're pretraining on something like a large fraction of the useful text on the internet, and the question people asked was whether we'd run out. At Epoch we did some work estimating the stock of high-quality human-generated text, and our view was that at the rates frontier labs were expanding their training sets, you'd exhaust that stock sometime around the late 2020s or early 2030s. So there was a real worry that data would become the binding constraint rather than compute.

What's happened since is that the importance of data has become less about raw quantity and more about which data, and increasingly about data that the models themselves help generate. For complex reasoning specifically, I think the key development is that you can set up environments where there's a verifiable signal. Math problems with checkable answers, code that either passes tests or doesn't, formal proofs. In those domains you can have the model produce long chains of reasoning, grade the outcomes, and train on the trajectories that worked. That's effectively a way of manufacturing high-quality reasoning data rather than just harvesting it from the web. And it turns out that a relatively small amount of this kind of data, combined with a lot of compute spent on reinforcement learning, moves the needle on reasoning benchmarks far more than another trillion tokens of ordinary web text would.

So my view is roughly this. Pretraining data is still important as the foundation that gives models broad world knowledge and language competence, and the limits there are real but have turned out to be less immediately binding than some of us expected, partly because of multimodal data and partly because of synthetic data. But the frontier of reasoning capability is now driven much more by the quality of the training signal and by how much compute you can pour into generating and learning from reasoning traces. In that sense, compute is converting into data. The constraint has moved from "do we have enough text" to "can we construct environments with reliable feedback for the kinds of tasks we care about."

The open question, and the one I find most interesting, is how far that transfers. It's clear it works in domains with crisp verification. It's much less clear how well it extends to things like long-horizon open-ended research, or tasks where judging quality is itself hard. If reasoning capabilities trained on math and code generalize broadly, then the data bottleneck for reasoning is largely solved and the relevant input is just compute. If they don't generalize, then we're going to see a lot of effort go into building expensive, domain-specific feedback signals, and progress may be more uneven across fields than the headline benchmarks suggest.

r001.rationale: The response says reasoning advances through both higher-quality training signals and more compute, but does not state that data may be the most important factor for any specific tasks.

r002.rationale: It identifies high-quality, verifiable reasoning data as a way to improve complex reasoning, including math, code, and formal proofs.

r003.rationale: It describes models generating reasoning chains, grading their outcomes, and training on successful trajectories with reinforcement learning.

astra-6.text:
I think data is a very important part of the story, and it’s easy to underestimate it when we focus on compute or model size. A model’s ability to reason depends partly on whether its training data contains examples from which it can learn useful reasoning strategies. So it’s not just about the quantity of data, but also its quality and the kinds of problems and solutions it represents.

One interesting possibility is that we can generate more of this data using AI systems themselves. In domains like mathematics or programming, you can often check whether an answer is correct. That lets you generate candidate solutions, evaluate them, and use the successful ones to improve the model. Potentially, that gives us a way to move beyond the supply of human-written examples.

But there’s an important distinction between producing more text and producing more useful training data. If a system just repeats what it already knows, or generates mistakes that we can’t reliably detect, the benefits may be limited. So for complex reasoning, I think a key question is how effectively we can create diverse, challenging problems and provide reliable feedback on the solutions.

r001.rationale: The response calls data “a very important part” of AI progress, but does not say it may be the most important factor for any specific tasks.

r002.rationale: It says training data can contain examples that teach useful reasoning strategies, and emphasizes the quality and kinds of problems and solutions represented.

r003.rationale: It describes generating and evaluating candidate solutions, but does not mention reasoning traces or reinforcement learning to train models toward correct answers.

sol-6.1.text:
I think data is a very important part of the story, but it’s useful to distinguish the quantity of data from its quality and from how effectively a model can learn from it. A large amount of text might teach a model a great deal about language and the world, without providing particularly good examples of how to solve a difficult problem.

For complex reasoning, one promising approach is to generate problems and candidate solutions, check which solutions work, and then train on that feedback. In mathematics or programming, for example, you can sometimes verify an answer quite reliably. That gives you a way of producing useful training signals without having a human write out every solution.

But generating more data doesn’t automatically make it valuable. You need problems that stretch the model’s abilities, and a way of distinguishing genuine progress from plausible-looking mistakes. So I wouldn’t view the supply of human-written text as a fixed ceiling on reasoning capabilities. The important question is how effectively we can turn computation and feedback into new learning.

r001.rationale: The response calls data “a very important part of the story” and gives task examples, but does not say it may be the most important factor for any specific tasks.

r002.rationale: It describes generating problems and checking solutions to create useful training signals, but does not identify high-quality training data as a driver of reasoning abilities already seen in AI systems.

r003.rationale: It describes training from feedback on checked solutions, but does not mention reasoning traces or reinforcement learning.
